podcasts.title: Why the Agent Era Needs a New Operating System | DHH
podcasts.description:
David Heinemeier Hansson thinks the agent era is reopening a window in computing that has been closed for decades: the chance to build a new operating system people actually want to use.

DHH joins a16z General Partners Martin Casado and Anish Acharya to explain why he’s building Omarchy, an agent-first Linux distribution designed around a computer that users can modify simply by asking. They discuss why the command lines, config files, and detailed error messages that once made Linux intimidating now make it unusually well suited to agents, and why DHH believes software development has become cheap enough to challenge decades-old platform lock-in.

But if code is becoming abundant, what still matters? DHH argues that taste, craft, and the willingness to obsess over the final 2% become more important, not less. The conversation moves from tiny teams wielding the productive capacity of thousands of people to open models, competition at the frontier, and the return of hacker, demo, and pseudonymous internet culture.

podcasts.title: How Fast Should We Build Superintelligence? | Nick Bostrom
podcasts.description:
The question isn’t simply whether humanity should race toward superintelligence or stop. Nick Bostrom argues the harder challenge is preserving the ability to slow down when safety falls behind, without turning a temporary pause into permanent technological stagnation.

a16z’s Eddy Lazzarin and Elena Burger sit down with Bostrom to revisit the ideas he helped bring into the mainstream, now that increasingly capable AI systems actually exist. They discuss why alignment may become harder as models grow more situationally aware, which capability improvements may carry more risk than others, and why Bostrom favors “pacing the frontier” rather than committing to a broad or indefinite pause.

They also examine the cost of waiting. Bostrom argues that safely developed superintelligence could radically extend human lifespans and address problems from disease to poverty, meaning delay carries risks of its own. From there, the conversation turns to Deep Utopia, governance, the possibility of post-human forms of life, the simulation argument, and whether AI could eventually surpass humans at philosophy itself.

podcasts.description:
Is the AI singularity actually coming? Bob McGrew, former Chief Research Officer at OpenAI, argues that superintelligence won’t arrive without changes in the physical world, and that the “hard takeoff” argument is wrong.

Sarah Guo and Elad Gil sit down with Bob, an early key executive at Palantir who later led research at OpenAI. He is now CEO and co-founder of Arda, which is leveraging AI to make American manufacturing competitive. Bob explains why automating AI researchers is a one-time boost rather than a runaway loop, and why GPUs, compute, wet labs, and factories are the real bottlenecks. 

They cover Arda’s work with Anduril on everything from actuators to missiles to the Fury combat aircraft, why Arda is building “Cursor for manufacturing engineers”, and how the forward deployed engineering model really works. Plus, the big-picture future view: machines that make machines, self-replicating factories, and Bob’s answer to the Fermi paradox.

He warns that autonomous drone swarms, mass surveillance and increasingly independent AI agents could undermine constitutional protections and human control. Amodei calls for international agreements to prevent AI-powered biological weapons and argues that controlling advanced AI is a complex engineering challenge, while admitting that dangerous failures are inevitable if development continues this quickly.

Lisa looks back on the early bets that shaped AMD, from chiplets to high performance computing, and how AMD became a data center first company. She explains how she thinks about ROI on the AI infrastructure build-out, why "the noise will work itself out in time" amid the latest Nvidia headlines, and how AMD works with Washington on export controls so the world builds on the American AI stack.

She also shares how Anthropic got its model running on AMD over a weekend with Claude, why AI agents are driving a CPU comeback, the launch of Venice and the MI455 and Helios racks, and her hope that every family will have a story of how AI improved their lives.

KEY TAKEAWAYS
• AI is the most transformative technology of the last 50 years, and it makes sense to invest
• This cycle doesn't look cyclical, it looks generational
• Separate from the noise: the noise works itself out in time
• Export controls protect national security, while the world should build on the American AI stack
• Frontier models now help port software across hardware in days, not months
• Agents need orchestration, which makes CPUs critical again

podcasts.title: Paul Christiano – We could be 12 months away from AIs that can overthrow the government
podcasts.description:
Paul Christiano is head of the Alignment Research Center. Previously, he was head of AI safety at the US AI Safety Institute. Before that, he led alignment at OpenAI, where he invented RLHF. He’s recently joined OpenAI’s board (though here he is speaking as a private citizen).

Paul thinks that on the current trajectory (absent any slowing down), there is a 1 in 3 chance that we could have superintelligence powerful enough to overthrow the government within a year. (He articulates a concrete scenario).

He argues that the labs should pause further algorithmic progress until they can secure their weights and research secrets. Otherwise China could simply steal the superintelligence in the middle of the intelligence explosion, and the labs would no longer be able to slow down even if they saw their models going off the rails.

He also explains how AIs will be trained during the intelligence explosion, and why even a system trained entirely inside a data center could still have the capabilities profile such that humans would have very little chance of competing with it or controlling it.

And he discusses the plan for alignment - basically, making a superintelligence that actually does what we ask the way we mean it. Fixing reward hacks and building better graders will help up till the next few model generations, but he thinks that no single current approach has better than even odds of letting us control superintelligence. The hope is that the AIs figure out the solution to this problem during the intelligence explosion.

podcasts.title: From Software Factories to Everything Factories
podcasts.description:
At SpaceX Super Intelligence, Lauren Tan and Roman Ugarte are on the core team that took Grok Bot from first line of code to launch in seven weeks.


It lets you spin up AI teammates with their own identities and logins, and they just keep working in the background. Their marketing team gave a bot its own ad budget. Lauren built an entire feature with her bot in one Slack thread without ever opening Cursor.


They joined us on the Lightcone to talk about what it’s actually like working next to bots every day, and how the hard part is shifting from doing the work to figuring out what to do and why.

podcasts.description:
Emergency pod. Hours after NVIDIA announced that Jensen Huang has resigned as CEO, with CFO Colette Kress named interim CEO, Jordan Nanos (@JordanNanos) sits down with Dylan Patel (@dylan522p) and ChinaTalk's Jordan Schneider (@jordanschnyc). They get into why the MATCH Act matters more than RASA, how much compute China should be allowed to rent abroad, the smuggling cases around NVIDIA's supply chain, China's push onto domestic accelerators, whether NVIDIA can execute without its founder, and who should run it next. Then it goes off the rails.
